title: Need help figuring out which RPG maker engine to use for my game

posts.author: Th3L1ttle3Man
posts.body:
I've been doing some work on a RPG maker that is based on One Piece, so far, I've run into multiple issues with RPG maker 2003 that makes it so that I can't implement certain things. I can't easily find very specific thing that each of the engines can do, so I figured consulting the forums would be the best shot. The main things that have been troubling for me is 1. Can't stack multiple separate states, for example: if I made a character poisoned, they couldn't be stunned 2. Can't have multiple moves that inflict the same state but with different chances to inflict the state 3. Have skills attack more than once (I want to have a move that can hit 5-8 times on different enemies)
Things that I'd like to have 1. One character equipping three weapons 2. items that can be used to deal damage and inflict states on enemies. I know I'm asking about a bunch of random things, but I was hoping that someone who knows more about specific engines that would make my game project work how I want it to. Thanks for at least reading this long post.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
There's really not a lot of differences between the editors' basic functionality - you're trying to use the oldest (well, newer version of the oldest) PC RPG Maker still sold.
I haven't looked at XP much, but everything from VX on can do all of your main things.
Your thing you'd like to have 2 can be done in any of them, and 1 can probably be done in any of the engines that support scripts - it can certainly be done in MV and MZ with plugins.
There's really not any reason
not
to simply get the newest software available. The farther back you go, the more you have to worry about compatibility with modern hardware and operating systems, and the loss from time of any scripts or resources that you can use to change mechanics like you want.
There's something to be said for the larger existing plugin library for MV over MZ, but your desired mechanics are simple enough that that doesn't really weigh in at all.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
If you are just starting out, I would get MZ as my first choice. MV as my second.
I have only used MZ, but from what I understand, MZ and MV are very similar. And from my experience, MZ is incredibly flexible.
Learning how to really use Event Commands, learning some JavaScript, using the MZ/MV Script Call reference, and plugins (as necessary), you can make almost anything you want. With some practical exceptions, of course.
Just spending some time looking at games in development here in this forum will show case some "non-typical" RM game designs and highlight just how flexible you can get.
But it also seems like you can get a lot more support for MZ/MV than you can for the older versions because there are more experienced users of MZ/MV who actively participate here and can help. The older the version, the harder it seems to find people who are active and experience with using them. There also seem to be far more tutorial resources for the newer versions than the older ones.
Good luck!

I would argue for MV but MZ is fine I guess. Put it on your Steam watchlist until it goes on sale, which it does around once a month, where it should be around $40.
It boils down to:
MV: Cheaper ($12 on sale), Yanfly plugins are cheaper than VisuStella, a lot more plugins in general
MZ: More QoL features in the engine itself, particularly the mapping.
However if you have both you can use MZ as a map editor for an MV project

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body: It's also relevant to note that MZ can deploy games for Apple computers, whereas MV games are not compatible with current MacOS versions.

posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body:
I use MV, but if I was starting out, and had a computer with the right specifications, I would go for MZ. It has a few goodies that you might not need immediately (such as being able to choose what layers to put tiles on), but will grow into being able to use. There are also minor enhancements to the editor, with some useful features.
The main attractions of MV are that it is possible to get a Linux version (through Steam), and you don't need such an up-to-date computer. It used to be that there were a lot more plugins for MV, but I am under the impression that that is not so much the case now.
The good news is that you can download a free trial of as many of the versions as you like. If I recall, they come with all the features, but stop working after a month if you don't buy the software and input the key you get.
